subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: accepting silently and working nights [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Sunaina, and I sit two desks from Omkar. When the manager asked for the feature by the end of the month, Omkar said "Sure" without opening the estimate sheet. After that Omkar was still at the desk when the cleaners arrived, and at midnight the chat status still glowed green. The testing part was quietly dropped. Two weeks later the release shipped, and by Monday three bugs were live and customers were writing in. At the review the manager said, "Good, so that timeline works. Let's keep this pace next time." Omkar nodded, dark circles under the eyes. I don't know why Omkar said yes without asking. But nobody outside our corner knew what it had cost.

qa.q: How many bugs were live by Monday?
qa.a: Three bugs were live by Monday.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling while nodding at the review?
qa.a: Omkar was probably exhausted and reluctant to admit the strain, judging by the dark circles under the eyes.

qa.q: What could Omkar do before answering the next deadline request, and why?
qa.a: Omkar could check the estimate first and say what fits, because a yes that ignores the numbers hides the real cost from the manager.

qa.q: How might the manager see the result of the release?
qa.a: The manager saw a feature delivered on time and so assumed the timeline was reasonable, without knowing about the late nights and dropped testing.

grounding: Illustrates a junior lead accepting a deadline in silence and working nights, so quality drops and the manager concludes the date was reasonable.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: accepting silently and working nights [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Rafiq's manager Shalini asked if the reporting dashboard could be ready in ten days. Rafiq, a new lead, didn't check anything. "Yes, no problem."
Wednesday night. It was midnight. Rafiq had skipped dinner and was writing queries with tired eyes. He hadn't told anyone the dashboard really needed about a month. His two teammates went home at seven; he didn't want to ask them for more.
Following Friday. He shipped on time, bleary-eyed. By Monday afternoon, three bugs had reached the live system: wrong totals for two regions and a chart that froze on phones. A client called Shalini.
Two weeks later. Shalini came to his desk, friendly. "You did that dashboard in ten days, so this new module should take about the same, right?"
Rafiq opened his mouth. He thought about the midnights, the bugs, the client call. "Sure," he said, and hated himself a little.

qa.q: How many bugs reached the live system?
qa.a: Three bugs reached the live system.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when Shalini asked about the new module?
qa.a: He felt trapped and a little self-hating, remembering the midnights and bugs but still saying 'Sure'.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Rafiq responded to the ten-day request?
qa.a: I would say 'Let me check' and break the work down before agreeing, then show Shalini the real estimate or smaller options.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini believes ten days was reasonable because the dashboard arrived on time, so she expects the same pace again.

grounding: Shows a junior lead accepting a deadline silently and working until midnight, causing bugs in production and teaching the manager the deadline was reasonable.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: accepting silently and working nights [Pitfall]
passage:
"Shreya, your manager asked for the portal in a week and you just said yes? Sit down. Let me, Shankar, tell you about my first lead job.
I was twenty-four. My manager asked if a customer portal could be done in eight days. I didn't count anything. I just said yes, because saying no felt like failing.
For eight nights I worked until two. I stopped writing tests. I skipped code reviews because there was no time. I delivered on the eighth day.
The next morning, customers couldn't reset their passwords. Then another bug, then another. The support team was furious.
And the worst part came a month later. My manager gave me an even bigger job with the same kind of deadline. Why wouldn't he? I had shown him it was possible.
Check the estimate first, Shreya. Every yes teaches your manager something."

qa.q: How many days was Shankar asked to build the customer portal in?
qa.a: Shankar was asked to build it in eight days.

qa.q: Why did young Shankar say yes without counting, and how did it feel?
qa.a: Saying no felt like failing, so Shankar agreed out of fear and then felt exhausted working until two every night.

qa.q: What was the key turning point in the story, and what should have been different?
qa.a: Saying yes without checking was the key choice; checking the estimate first would have avoided the bugs and the bigger unrealistic deadline later.

qa.q: How might the support team have felt when the bugs appeared?
qa.a: The support team was furious, likely overwhelmed by customers who couldn't reset their passwords.

grounding: Shows a junior lead accepting a deadline without checking and working nights, leading to bugs in production and an even harder deadline next time.
